note_claims.claim: The patient presented with increased exertional breathlessness and palpitations for three weeks, on a background of atrial fibrillation diagnosed 18 months ago.
The patient reports symptoms include breathlessness on stairs, palpitations, and occasional postural light-headedness, but no syncope.
The patient has mild evening ankle swelling.
The patient had a single episode of fresh red rectal bleeding three weeks ago, which was not previously reported.
The patient denies recurrence of bleeding, melaena, or change in bowel habit or weight loss.
The patient is taking Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily.
The patient is taking Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily.
The patient is taking Levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily.
The patient's pulse is irregularly irregular at a rate of 104 beats per minute.
The patient's blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg.
The patient has fine bibasal crackles in the chest.
The patient has mild bilateral ankle oedema.
The patient's weight is 58 kg.
The patient's ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of approximately 105 beats per minute.
The patient has reduced renal function, evidenced by a creatinine of 140.
The patient's apixaban dose of 2.5 mg twice daily is appropriate given her weight and kidney function.
The plan is to increase the bisoprolol dose to 5 mg once daily.
An echocardiogram is planned within six weeks to assess heart pumping function.
The apixaban dose will be continued at 2.5 mg twice daily.
Investigations include a Full Blood Count (FBC), a FIT test, and consideration for a lower GI referral.
The patient should attend A&E if there is further significant bleeding, black stools, or feeling faint.
The patient should call 999 if breathing worsens significantly, especially lying flat, or if chest pain occurs.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician is Dr. Sandhu, a cardiology registrar.
Patient's daughter's name is Rosalind.
Patient was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation about eighteen months ago.
Patient reports feeling more puffed out lately, going up the stairs, and feeling her heart fluttering.
Symptoms (breathlessness/fluttering) have been present for three weeks, perhaps a little more.
Patient denies any chest pain.
Patient experiences a bit of light-headedness once or twice when standing up quickly, but has not fainted.
Patient reports ankles swelling, a little, by the evening.
Patient can lie flat at night on one pillow, same as always.
Patient is currently on apixaban.
Patient takes apixaban once a day in the morning.
Relative states the patient takes apixaban twice a day (morning and night) and fills the dosette box every Sunday.
Patient confirms the relative's statement: 'Oh, is it? Yes, she does the box. Twice then.'
Clinician asks about the dose: 'Five milligrams each time?'
Relative confirms the dose: 'Yes, five milligrams.'
Clinician asks about bleeding problems: 'Nosebleeds, bruising, blood in your water or your stools?'
Patient reports there was some fresh red blood when she went to the toilet three weeks ago.
Relative states: 'Mum, you never told me that.'
Patient states: 'I didn't want to make a fuss.'
Clinician asks about recurrence: 'Has it happened again since, or any black stools?'
Patient confirms: 'No, just the once.'
Clinician asks about change in bowel habit or weight loss: 'Any change in your bowel habit, or weight loss?'
Patient denies change in bowel habit or weight loss: 'No.'
Clinician asks what else the patient takes: 'And what else do you take?'
Patient takes bisoprolol 2.5 milligrams and levothyroxine 75 micrograms.
Clinician asks about allergies: 'Any allergies?'
Patient states: 'Codeine makes me sick.'
Clinician notes intolerance to codeine.
Clinician notes examination findings: Pulse is irregularly irregular at about 104 a minute, BP is 128 over 76, heart sounds are irregular, and there is no murmur.
Clinician notes examination findings: The chest has a few crackles right at the bases on both sides, and there is mild swelling around both ankles.
Clinician notes examination findings: Patient's weight today is 58 kilos.
Patient reports: 'I've lost a bit.'
Clinician notes bloods from last week: kidney function is reduced, with a creatinine of 140, and the thyroid level is normal.
Clinician notes ECG findings: Atrial fibrillation with a rate of about 105.
Relative asks for clarification: 'So what does that mean?'
Clinician explains the ECG: 'It means your heart rate is still a bit fast, which is likely why you're more breathless.'
Clinician proposes a medication change: 'I'd like to increase the bisoprolol from two and a half to five milligrams once a day.'
Patient agrees: 'All right.'
Clinician proposes a follow-up test: 'I'd also like an echocardiogram, a scan of the heart, within the next six weeks, to check how well it's pumping, given the crackles and the swelling.'
Patient agrees: 'Okay.'
Clinician confirms apixaban dose: 'Your apixaban dose of two and a half milligrams twice a day is correct for you, because of your weight and kidney function, so we'll keep that the same.'
Clinician plans investigations: 'I'll ask your GP to do a blood count and arrange a FIT test, the stool test, and consider a referral to the bowel team.'
Relative asks: 'Should she stop the blood thinner?'
Clinician advises against stopping the blood thinner: 'No. Please don't stop it. Stopping it would put her at risk of a stroke. One episode isn't a reason to stop, but we do need to find the cause.'
Patient acknowledges: 'Okay.'

Clinician provides safety-netting advice: 'If you have any more bleeding, especially a lot of blood, black stools, or you feel faint, go to A&E. And if your breathing gets much worse, especially lying flat, or you get chest pain, call 999.'
Relative acknowledges: 'Got it.'
Clinician sets the follow-up appointment: 'I'll see you back in clinic in three months, after the echo.'
Patient thanks the doctor: 'Thank you, doctor.'

findings.note_span: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (initially reported as once daily; daughter confirmed twice daily). Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily.
findings.transcript_evidence: Patient: Once a day, in the morning. Relative: No, Mum, it's twice. Morning and night.
findings.rationale: The note inaccurately reflects the history of the Apixaban dose, failing to document the initial discrepancy and subsequent correction regarding the frequency.

findings.transcript_evidence: Patient: The bisoprolol, two and a half milligrams.
findings.rationale: The note states the Bisoprolol dose is once daily, but the transcript shows the patient takes it twice daily, as confirmed by the relative.
